title: Trump aggressively pushed his party to redraw electoral maps. How much did that backfire?
content: When President Donald Trump launched his brazen mid-decade redistricting gambit in Texas last year, he confidently declared that Republicans were “ entitled to five more seats ” in the Lone Star State. Of course, the GOP wasn’t entitled to anything. And the midterms offered a swift reality check. In last week’s election, the party lost 4 of the 5 Texas seats it gerrymandered for itself last year. But it wasn’t just Texas. Republicans have won only 2 of the 15 districts they tried to rig for themselves, according to CNN’s redistricting tracker. One more seat, in Louisiana, is going to a runoff. And all told, the gambit actually cost them seats, after the map they redrew in North Carolina spread the party too thin and allowed Democrats to flip at least a half-dozen GOP seats. Democrats were also able to win a handful of additional seats in California when they fought back with their own redraw. There’s a prevailing narrative that Trump’s redistricting gambit backfired on the GOP — and pretty badly. But while there’s no question the plot was costly in 2026, it’s too early to say it won’t help Republicans over the long term. How could that be? And what’s next in the redistricting battles? We’re still waiting for some results — and there’s some subjectivity involved in how you count wins and losses when it comes to redistricted seats — but right now it’s clear Republicans actually lost seats from the ploy. The GOP gained one seat in Texas and another in Tennessee. But Democrats are set to flip five seats in California, six or seven in North Carolina and three in Ohio. They also flipped two GOP districts in Texas and they have a narrow lead in a district in Tennessee that Republicans diluted to make another district more winnable. So, all told, Republicans redrew 15 districts for themselves, compared to just five for Democrats. But if current results hold, Democrats could gain a net of 16 seats from the states that were redrawn in this redistricting fight. (Democrats also gained a seat in Utah, due to a court-ordered redraw of that state’s map.) There has been plenty of talk since the election about how all of these maps backfired on Republicans. But that’s not strictly true. North Carolina clearly backfired — at least in this election and at the congressional level — but other maps like Florida’s and Texas’ merely failed to live up to GOP hopes. Republicans didn’t lose seats in Florida and Texas because they redrew the maps; they just didn’t win the ones they’d hoped. Republicans still won 63% of Texas’ districts despite losing every statewide race. And in Florida, Republicans still won 71% of the districts even though the statewide contests were close. There is a term for when a gerrymander backfires by spreading your voters too thin and allowing the other party to win a bunch of districts: a “dummymander.” That really only happened in North Carolina. But in a twist, local Republicans that declined to go along with Trump’s gambit actually saved the GOP from itself in this election. According to an analysis from Decision Desk HQ , attempted Republican redraws could’ve jeopardized an additional district in South Carolina and six more in Indiana — leading to a potential wipeout in the Hoosier State. Trump was furious with GOP state senators who voted against these maps. He targeted and unseated a number of Indiana state legislators in the primaries. It turned out they were doing him a favor. They prevented two more dummymanders. But even when it comes to these maps that failed or even backfired in 2026, it’s worth taking the long view. Just because they didn’t work or even hurt this time doesn’t mean it will always be thus, or that the whole thing will have been a bust. It’s quite possible — even likely — that in closer elections in 2028 and 2030, Republicans would win back many of those seats in North Carolina and pick off more of the ones they aimed for in Alabama, Florida, Ohio and Texas. A lot of these districts favored Trump by double-digits, after all. If that does happen, the GOP would have gained a fair amount of seats from this process, in the end. And the party would probably declare that to be worth it. After all, the current Democratic gains basically just mean the already-huge new Democratic majority will be about 11 seats bigger — around 260-175 instead of around 250-185 seats. As things stand, the redistricting process moved the median House district about two points to the right — so that it’s a district Trump won by about five points in 2024, rather than by three points. That wasn’t enough to withstand the Democrats’ biggest popular vote win in half a century, but it should still help plenty long term. That’s if things stay where they are. But the newly empowered state-level Democrats could finish what Republicans started by redrawing some more maps — and bringing this whole process something closer to long-term parity. After previously facing legal obstacles to redrawing maps in Maryland, New York and Virginia, Democrats could move forward with redraws ahead of the 2028 election that could hand them a significant number of new seats in those states. Democrats could also draw new maps in states where they just landed “trifectas” of control — the governorship and both chambers of the state legislature. Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley has already said he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map. Another possibility would seem to be Minnesota. The GOP has far fewer apparent opportunities to draw more seats. It could be dicey politically for Democrats to jump back into redrawing maps. But Republicans clearly started it and drew many more seats for themselves. And if Democrats don’t take advantage of what opportunities they have, this whole exercise could still benefit the GOP — even though it clearly didn’t do Trump, the person who pushed it so hard in the first place, much good.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a significant and substantiated development in the category of people/politics, providing clear evidence of the consequences of Trump's redistricting gambit, including the loss of seats by the GOP and gain of seats by the Democrats.

title: Customers report service outages at major US banks
content:
Thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, have reported trouble accessing services.
Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems may have been behind the glitch and noted the impacts may have affected other banks. It added the issue was "temporary" and not "systemic" or "cyber-related".
Problems appeared to be easing for many customers by early Monday evening.
The issue comes after a string of unrelated technical problems, including a massive Microsoft outage , a network failure that grounded all US flights , and United Airlines reporting a "widespread system outage".
Problems started on Monday afternoon. There were almost 5,000 reports of problems with Chase Bank's services, according to the Downdetector website.
Clients reported issues accessing their online accounts, viewing balances and performing transactions, like bank transfers and wire transfers, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.
A Chase Bank customer in Texas told the outlet that he could not deposit a check at a Dallas branch on Monday, reporting that he was told his transaction could not be completed. He said a bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" but did not provide additional details.
Chase Bank told its customers that "some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete" but they still had "access to their accounts and funds".
The bank, a subsidiary of JP Morgan Chase, serves more than 86m customers at 5,000 branches across the US, as well as 7.4m small businesses, according to the company's webpage. It is also the top credit card issuer in the US.
The exact nature of the bug was unclear. The BBC has contacted Chase Bank.
Bank of America customers had issues at ATMs and using mobile banking services online, while US Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app, CBS reported.
Customers using another institution, US Bank, also reported issues transferring funds and Wells Fargo customers said they had problems signing into their accounts, getting account balances and making transactions.
US Bank said some its systems were not directly affected but clients using the Zelle, a digital payment platform, received error messages saying their payments could not be sent.
Zelle has said its service is "operating as it should" and issues at other banks could be affecting payments.
Customers also reported issues with Truist, PNC and Capital One but all these companies told the BBC they have not been impacted.
As of 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), Chase, Bank of America and US Bank had seen a fall in the number of reported outages.
Just as the banking issue affected US customers on Monday, United Airlines confirmed a "widespread system outage", which it described as "a technology issue affecting departing flights".
That issue resolved within a few hours.
The Chicago-based airline did not say what is believed to have caused the issue, but a spokesperson said it is not related to cybersecurity.
The issue did not appear to be affecting any other airlines.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a category-specific development (a widespread service outage at major US banks) and provides a clear reason for readers to care (impact on thousands of customers, disruption to daily transactions)

title: Kidnap, child marriage and poverty: Why millions of Nigerian children can't go to school
content:
As she pounds millet, 15-year-old Hadiza sings the English alphabet. It is a reminder of something that she desperately misses - going to school.
"Sometimes I write on the ground to practise and see if I'm still writing correctly," she says.
One night, about two years ago, a group of armed men raided her village.
"They scared our cattle away and abducted a girl. We had to run away. We walked barefoot all the way here," she says.
Since then she has lived in a displaced persons camp in Goronyo, a few kilometres from her home. For a short while she went to school here, but soon met a young man and, at the age of 13, stopped going to classes and got married.
"It's tradition here that once a girl is married, her education ends," she explains.
Now she lives with her in-laws and helps look after the home.
Although Nigerian law prohibits marriage under the age of 18, it is not always enforced.
Hadiza is one of nearly 19 million children in Nigeria who are missing out on an education, according to estimates shared by Unesco in 2024. That's about one in four of the country's school-age children.
Against this backdrop, the BBC World Service has launched Dars Hausa, an educational programme in the main language spoken in northern Nigeria, as well as neighbouring Niger, Cameroon and elsewhere in West Africa.
It brings English, maths and science lessons to children across West Africa, via social media, local television partnerships and radio. Many people in the region get their news from the radio and nearly half of households in Nigeria have one, according to the charity Save the Children.
Dars means "lesson" in Pashto and Dari, and it was first launched in those languages in 2023 for Afghan children barred from attending school. An Arabic version followed in February 2025.
The reasons why so many Nigerian children are out of school are numerous and complex. Like Hadiza, 12-year-old Rukayya also lives in the displacement camp in Goronyo.
"It pains me to see other children studying and going to school while I cannot," she says.
As the eldest child, each day Rukayya goes out to gather firewood to sell and to beg so that her younger siblings can have something to eat.
"If my father was alive, I wouldn't have to go out and beg," she explains, saying some people mock her "but it doesn't stop me because it is our only way to survive."
Bandits killed her father about a year ago in front of her, she says, and her family fled from their home to the camp.
She and Hadiza are among 670,000 people in north-west and central Nigeria who have been forced from their homes by armed robbery and kidnappings, according to the International Organization for Migration.
Some attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by criminal gangs, known in Nigeria as bandits, who steal, kill and kidnap.
The school that Hadiza once attended in Goronyo is the only one serving children in the camp and typically has about 50 students in each class.
ranking_reason: The article reports a meaningful, substantive development relevant to its category, 'people', and is publishable.

analysis.reason: The article reports a meaningful, substantive development relevant to its category, 'people', and is publishable.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a substantive, meaningful development relevant to its category, 'people', and provides a clear reason for readers to care. The story highlights the plight of millions of Nigerian children missing out on education due to poverty, child marriage, and kidnapping, and introduces the Dars Hausa program as a potential solution. The article provides personal stories and statistics to illustrate the problem, making it a valuable and engaging read.
